tweets.text: RT @DavidNage: Two different SEC things could happen tomorrow (Friday). People are already mixing them up, so: THE ONE THAT'S SCHEDULED 10am ET, open meeting, webcast on https://t.co/KFnX8QZfmQ. The Commission votes on whether to propose Regulation Crypto Assets. This is about how tokens get issued and sold in the first place — a legal path to sell a token to Americans without doing a full securities registration. It's run by the division that handles offerings and disclosure, which tells you the scope: issuance, not trading. What I'll be reading for: — Can a token ever stop being a security? — Is one federal filing enough, or do you still deal with all fifty states? — How much can you raise, from whom, and what do you have to disclose? — Once someone buys, can they sell? Important: this is a proposal, not a rule. Comment period, probably a revision, then a vote to adopt. Nothing changes tomorrow. THE ONE THAT MIGHT SHOW UP Bloomberg reported Monday the SEC is also working on relief for tokenized stocks (the "innovation exemption") — real stocks like Apple or Tesla, traded on a blockchain, potentially around the clock. Details could come tomorrow. This is NOT on the meeting agenda. If it lands it'll come through a different mechanism, and depending on how it's built it could take effect much faster than the proposal above. The question I'd read for: does the company have to agree before its stock gets tokenized? A version that requires consent looks very different from one that doesn't. That exact provision is what stalled this back in May, when exchanges pushed back.
